newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Apartheid leader Malan to hear fate on Friday.
newsitem.headline: Apartheid leader Malan to hear fate on Friday.

text.p: South Africa's apartheid-era defence minister, General Magnus Malan, will hear his fate on Friday at the end of an eight-month murder trial relating to a massacre of 13 blacks nine years ago.

Friends of the old white minority regime and anti-apartheid activists alike are eagerly awaiting an important verdict for a young South African democracy trying to come to terms with its troubled past.
Malan, the most senior apartheid leader to stand trial for atrocities, will be buoyed by the acquittal of six of his 15 co-defendants on Thursday.

Supreme court judge Jan Hugo found them not guilty of any of the charges brought against them by the state, which was trying to prove they were responsible for the 1987 death squad killing of 13 people in KwaMakutha near the port of Durban.
The six were policemen in the KwaZulu-Natal black homeland run by Inkatha Freedom Party leader Mangosuthu Buthelezi until it was scrapped after all-race elections in April 1994.
Inkatha on Thursday hailed their acquittal as "a triumph of justice".
"The state should in future be more prudent and cautious before embarking on prosecutions which are widely perceived to have high-level political connotations," it said in a statement.
But the rival African National Congress of President Nelson Mandela called the verdict a travesty.

"In the eyes of the our people, the prosecution team failed them. This will have far reaching consequences. It is doubtful whether our people will ever have confidence in the judicial system if it remains the same," the ANC said.

Senior members of the movement have previously lamented the fact that most of South Africa's judges are white men appointed during the apartheid era, and have accused some of them of administering racially-biased justice in the past.
ANC officials have also accused the chief prosecutor in the Malan trial, Tim McNally, of failing to go after perpetrators of apartheid crimes with enough enthusiasm.

The six acquitted on Thursday were alleged to have been members of the death squad which had been recruited from 206 Inkatha men trained by the military to protect Buthelezi and his party against attacks from the ANC and its allies.
The acquittals bring to 10 the number of accused freed by Hugo out of the original 20 men charged with murder, attempted murder and conspiracy to murder.
Hugo said in his summary of the trial that the prosecution's three key witnesses were liars and unreliable, adding the prosecution had failed to call witnesses who could have strengthened its case.
He also criticised police investigation methods and said some of their testimony in court was "misleading".

The prosecution has not directly linked Malan and three of his accused generals to the massacre, but has relied on top secret documents detailing military proposals to train an offensive unit for Inkatha to prove a conspiracy-to-murder charge.

Hugo said some evidence supported the view that Malan and the generals had no links with the attack, which the defence called a "frolic" run solely by Johan Opperman, an ex-officer turned state witness who commanded the attack.

An analyst from the independent Institute of Democracy said if Malan was acquitted, people would lose faith in the ability of the justice system to prosecute those who masterminded atrocities under apartheid and those who carried them out.
"The hurts of the past are not going to be adequately healed if Malan gets off," said Eric Apelgren.
